title: Counting Pots from the Pavement
passage:
Stand across the road from a terrace and count the pots along one stack. Under each is a separate flue dropping to its own grate, and the pots seldom match. Pattern tells you very little. Builders’ yards sold whatever was in stock, householders bought ornament to tell their own door from thirty identical ones, and a stack rebuilt in 1961 carries what came off the lorry. Height is the part worth reading. The pot that stands a course above its neighbours belongs to a flue that smoked, usually the shortest one on the stack, the flue from the attic bedroom, with the least warm air beneath it to do the lifting. Narrowing the mouth helps as well, since the same gases leave faster through less of an opening. A pot is bedded in a flaunching of mortar, so a sweep could try a taller one without calling a bricklayer.
– Silas Ludderby, writing on the architecture of ordinary streets

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about the pots on a single stack?

options.text: A pot raised above the others marks a flue that had been drawing badly.
The narrowed mouth on a pot is mainly there to shut out rain and birds.
Pattern and ornament on a stack record which flue below gave the most trouble.
They were picked to match the ridge tiles and the brickwork of the house below.

questions.rationale: The answer follows directly from 'The pot that stands a course above its neighbours belongs to a flue that smoked, usually the shortest one on the stack, the flue from the attic bedroom, with the least warm air beneath it to do the lifting.' A recasts that in different words - a pot standing higher than its neighbours belongs to the flue that had been drawing badly - and adds nothing the passage does not supply ('smoked' is the passage's word for a flue that draws badly, and the sentence supplies the reason: the least warm air beneath it to do the lifting). B is the causal-glue trap built on the commonest lay belief about anything fitted to the top of a chimney: that the narrowing is a weather and vermin measure. The passage assigns the narrowing a different job entirely - 'the same gases leave faster through less of an opening' - and never mentions rain, birds or a cowl. C is the true-idea-from-the-wrong-place trap: it keeps the passage's real proposition (something about the stack records which flue misbehaved) and attaches it to the feature the passage explicitly disqualifies. 'Pattern tells you very little' is flat, and the following sentence gives three non-diagnostic causes of pattern - builders'-yard stock, householders telling their own door from thirty identical ones, a 1961 rebuild. A solver who has read only the first half of the passage takes C. D is the plausible-outside-knowledge trap: real chimney pots are terracotta and matching them to brick and ridge tiles is a sensible real-world thought, but the passage says nothing about matching, and what it does say about ornament runs the other way, since householders bought it to tell one door from thirty identical ones.

generator_meta.mechanism_verification_note: BUILDING-SCIENCE CHECK, run 2026-09-01 BEFORE drafting (the batch15 TYPE-001 short was refuted at V-FINAL for stating a mechanism backwards; not repeated). Instrument: WebSearch plus one WebFetch, logged honestly including the fetch that did NOT support what its title promised. (1) Query 'chimney pot narrows outlet increases velocity flue gases improves draught why pots differ on one stack' returned thelocalchimneysweep.co.uk 'The Chimney Pot: An Examination of Function, History, and Architectural Significance in Britain' and related trade pages: as flue gases pass through the narrowed outlet of a pot their velocity increases (continuity / Venturi), enhancing the upward pull, and this can improve draught more effectively than adding the same height in plain masonry. Supports the passage's 'Narrowing the mouth helps as well, since the same gases leave faster through less of an opening.' The same source supplies the multi-flue fact (several pots on one stack indicate several fireplaces on different floors sharing the stack) and the honest counter-explanation the passage concedes: the Victorian era was the 'Golden Age' of chimney pots largely because identical terraces led householders to use pots to personalise them, with suppliers offering over 300 designs and strong regional naming. That counter-explanation is why the passage says pattern tells you little rather than pretending ornament had no role. (2) Query on taller pots and downdraught returned the 3-2-10 rule and the standard account: where a nearby roofline or obstruction puts the terminal inside the turbulence zone, or where free circulation is poor, extra height compensates, and taller pots are used in closely built settings to discharge above the obstruction. (3) Query on short flues and stack effect returned en.wikipedia 'Stack effect' (buoyancy force rises with the height of the column and the thermal difference) and trade pages stating that a pot raises the level of the outlet, lengthens the column of hot gases and so enhances natural draught. Together these give the passage's direction: the shortest flue on a stack, the attic grate, has the shortest warm column, draws worst and is the one given extra height. (4) NEGATIVE RESULT, logged rather than buried: WebFetch on rejpipeschimneysweepservices.com 'The Height of Chimney Pots: Why They Vary and Why It Matters' confirmed only the generic claims (taller pots often produce a stronger draft; height compensates for rooflines, trees and adjacent buildings) and explicitly did NOT address within-one-stack height variation, whether a taller pot fixes poor draw, flaunching, or outlet narrowing. The within-stack inference is therefore MINE, built from documented physics (draught scales with warm-column height; a short flue has the shortest column) and not quoted from a source that states it in those words; flagged here for the pedagogy and V-FINAL reviewers rather than presented as sourced. (5) Query on flaunching returned buildingconservation.com 'Chimneys and Flues', SPAB chimney maintenance and trade pages: flaunching is the mortar bedding at the head of the stack into which pots are bedded, and a pot is replaced by taking off the failed flaunching, bedding and aligning the new pot and forming new weathered flaunching, with the brickwork below left alone unless itself defective. Supports 'A pot is bedded in a fillet of mortar, so a sweep could try a taller one without calling a bricklayer' - note the passage says a SWEEP could try one, a trade claim about who does the work, which is the softest assertion in the piece and is not what any option turns on.

edits.from:
Stand across the road from a terrace and count the pots along one stack. Behind each is a separate flue dropping to its own grate, and the pots seldom match. Pattern tells you very little. Builders’ yards sold whatever was in stock, householders bought ornament to tell their own door from thirty identical ones, and a stack rebuilt in 1961 carries what came off the lorry. Height is the part worth reading. The pot that stands a course above its neighbours belongs to a flue that smoked, usually the shortest one on the stack, the flue from the attic bedroom, with the least warm air beneath it to do the lifting. Narrowing the mouth helps as well, since the same gases leave faster through less of an opening. A pot is bedded in a fillet of mortar, so a sweep could try a taller one without calling a bricklayer.
– Silas Ludderby, writing on the architecture of ordinary streets
